opus-5.5.text:
I think this is one of the most important judgment calls for any team right now. My honest view is that continuing to push reasoning benchmarks inside the chat paradigm has diminishing returns. That doesn't mean the work is useless. Better reasoning is a foundation for everything that comes next. But if you only optimize for scores on math competitions or coding puzzles in a single-turn, question-and-answer format, you can end up very good at a game that is slowly becoming less relevant.

The chat paradigm assumes a human asks, the model thinks, and the model answers. The interaction is short and the human closes the loop. What we're moving toward is the model acting more like an agent. It works over long horizons, uses tools, interacts with real environments, gets feedback from the world rather than from a grader, and corrects itself. The capabilities that matter there are a bit different. Long-context coherence, planning, recovering from mistakes, knowing when to stop or ask. A lot of those aren't captured by today's reasoning benchmarks at all.

So in terms of resource allocation, I'd keep a solid investment in reasoning, because you can't build agents on a weak reasoning core. But the marginal compute and the best people should increasingly go toward the next paradigm: building environments, building scalable feedback signals, and figuring out RL over long trajectories. That's harder. The evaluation is messier, and you don't get a clean number to put in a press release. But I think that's exactly where the real differentiation will come from.

There's also a cultural point. Benchmarks are comforting because they give you a clear target. A research team that only chases leaderboards can lose the ability to ask what the model should actually be able to do. I'd rather we accept some uncertainty and bet on where the paradigm is going than be the best at the one that's ending.

r001.rationale: The candidate argues that benchmark gains have diminishing returns, but it does not mention a score around sixty or seventy points or say that such a score is sufficient.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the two aren't as separate as the question makes them sound, but if you force me to choose, I lean toward the next paradigm, and I'll try to explain why.

Benchmarks within the chat paradigm are useful. They gave us a shared yardstick and let the whole field move fast. But I think we've reached the point where a few more points on a math or coding leaderboard tells you less and less about whether the model is actually becoming more capable in the world. A lot of that improvement is now coming from targeted data, from knowing what the evaluation looks like, from reinforcement learning on verifiable problems. That's real engineering, but it is also a kind of local optimization. You can climb very high on that hill and still not be standing anywhere near the next one.

What I mean by "the next paradigm" is a model that doesn't just answer a question in one turn, but can operate over long horizons, interact with an environment, make mistakes, observe the result, and correct itself. The chat paradigm is fundamentally a model talking to a person. The next one is a model doing work, where the feedback comes from reality rather than from a human judging the reply. That changes what you train on, how you evaluate, and frankly what "intelligence" means for the system.

The reason I don't think you can simply skip the first and jump to the second is that reasoning is the foundation. An agent that can't reason reliably over many steps will fail quickly in a long task, and the failures compound. So the reasoning work isn't wasted. The question is what you optimize it for. If you optimize for the final answer on a static benchmark, you get one kind of model. If you optimize for the process, for the ability to verify your own intermediate steps and to know when you don't know, you get something that transfers much better into agentic settings.

So my practical view is this. Keep investing in reasoning, but shift the target away from scores and toward the properties the next paradigm needs: robustness over long trajectories, calibration, the ability to use tools and recover from errors. And at the same time, be willing to spend real compute and real research effort on things that won't show up on today's leaderboards for a while. That's uncomfortable, especially for a company, because the benchmark is where the attention is. But historically the teams that defined the next paradigm were the ones who were a bit early and a bit unmeasured, not the ones who were squeezing the last few points out of the current one.

One more thing. I think there's a risk of over-romanticizing "the next paradigm" as if it's a single clean idea waiting to be discovered. It usually isn't. It tends to emerge from a lot of small, unglamorous infrastructure work, from environments, from data pipelines, from evaluation that's much harder to build than a question bank. So the right attitude is probably less "chase the paradigm" and more "build the conditions in which it can appear," while being honest with yourself about when the benchmark gains have stopped meaning what they used to.

r001.rationale: The response argues that further benchmark gains have diminishing value and recommends shifting focus, but it does not suggest that roughly 60 or 70 points is a sufficient score.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think it’s a strict either-or choice. Improving reasoning within the chat paradigm still matters. But we have to distinguish between getting a higher benchmark score and expanding what a model can actually do. Those can overlap, but they’re not necessarily the same thing.

The question I would ask is: what is the model still unable to do, even if we keep improving its reasoning scores? If the limitation is that it can’t interact with an environment, learn from feedback, or carry a task through over time, then a better answer in a chat window may only solve part of the problem. We need to explore changes to the training process and the way the model acts, not just the way it responds.

At the same time, pursuing the next paradigm shouldn’t mean abandoning concrete measurement. You need a hypothesis about what new capability becomes possible and an experiment that can test it. Otherwise, “the next paradigm” is just a phrase.

So I would keep advancing reasoning, while making room for experiments that might change the formulation of the problem. The most interesting direction is where those efforts connect—where stronger reasoning enables something beyond answering a harder question.

r001.rationale: The response discusses benchmark scores generally but gives no roughly 60–70 point threshold or suggestion that reaching it may be sufficient.

sol-6.1.text:
I don’t think those are mutually exclusive, but we should distinguish between improving a model’s capabilities and improving its benchmark scores. A higher reasoning score can reflect real progress, but it doesn’t automatically tell us whether the model can solve an open-ended problem, learn from feedback, or work reliably over a long period.

The chat paradigm is still useful. It gives us a way to study reasoning and understand where models fail. But if we organize all our research around answering a question in a chat box, we may overlook capabilities that require interaction with an environment.

So I would keep improving reasoning while also asking what those improvements make possible beyond chat. Can the model take an action, observe the result, revise its approach, and finish a task? The next paradigm may emerge from developing that whole loop. We shouldn’t wait until every existing benchmark is saturated before exploring it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses improving reasoning benchmarks and exploring beyond chat, but it never suggests that a score around 60 or 70 points may be sufficient.
